title: Fifa says 'nobody selling football' as plan continues
description: Football's governing body Fifa plans to continue the consultation process after Uefa threatens to boycott World Cups.
fullText:
Fifa says that "nobody is selling football" as it vowed to continue with the controversial plan to sell stakes in its competitions to private investors.

Uefa - the body that governs European football - voted on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plan proceeded.

Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, said its 41 member associations also "rejected" the proposal made by Fifa president Gianni Infantino.

Fifa oversees world football and Infantino would need 106 of its 211 members to vote in favour for the proposal to go through. Uefa and Concacaf members combined make up 96 of those votes.

In a statement released on Friday, Fifa claimed the consultation process had been "disrupted by incorrect media reports".

"We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation," the statement read.

"We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each MA (member association) has the ability to express its vote based on facts.

"Nobody is selling football. This is not something Fifa would ever entertain."

Is Infantino finished? Could Uefa boycott World Cup? What happens now?

Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approved

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Fifa wants to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors will be able to buy stakes in it.

It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it is made clear that Fifa's tournaments will expand to hit an estimated increased pay-out of 24m euros per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.

It mentions "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".

The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".

There is no mention in the document of the women's game.

On Friday, Fifa said FFE had been proposed "to ensure all Fifa member associations have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries".

"This does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of Fifa or football itself," it added.

Infantino previously wrote to Fifa members saying they will receive $40m (£30m) if they back his controversial proposal. He set a deadline of 19 September for federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).

However, Uefa has accused Fifa of using football "to enrich themselves and their friends".

If approval is granted, Fifa says Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Uefa and Concacaf have led the opposition to Infantino's plan.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product," Uefa's statement on Thursday read.

"It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent.

"No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa's duty as the custodian of world football."

Concacaf said its members "expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal" and the "artificially short deadline imposed".

It also questioned the need for private investment after what Fifa claimed was the most profitable World Cup in history.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said that it is "deeply concerned that Fifa's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football".

The AFC also said it was "unacceptable" that it had not been consulted before the proposal was publicly announced, nor provided with "detailed governance, financial or legal analysis".

The governing body overseeing football in South America, Conmebol, is yet to publicly comment on the proposals. The governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) have said they will discuss Fifa's plan in August.

Chelsea manager and 2010 World Cup winner Xabi Alonso was asked about the situation during his side's pre-season tour of Australia.

"I think that football has to be for the people, not in private hands and I think that the way we love it is this way and we have seen a great World Cup and it's good to defend the interests of all the people," he said.

"Hopefully it won't happen and we will do it - we will keep the game as attractive and as authentic as we like it and that's why it creates these emotions, these passions."

It feels as though no-one who matters knows how this situation is going to play out just yet.

"Not sure the detail was considered when deciding the overall policy," was the response from a senior European football source when asked what this decision means for the U20 Women's World Cup, starting on 5 September, being hosted by Poland and featuring plenty of European nations.

Uefa's boycott threat will be activated if Infantino's funding deal is accepted.

Given 19 September is the deadline for countries to accept Fifa's deal and bank $20m (£15m) on 1 January, in theory, countries could be pulling out of that tournament in the middle of the quarter-finals and before the semis.

After that, the next senior matches in a Fifa competition are the Women's World Cup play-offs in October, which feature England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland among others.

Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. The Swiss is due to stand for a fourth term in March.

Prior to this week, it had been anticipated he would be re-elected unopposed. FAs around the world, including some in Europe, have already confirmed their intention to support the 56-year-old.

But sources say in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.

While Uefa members are among the richest on the planet, many nations elsewhere rely on Fifa funding for basic infrastructure.

"There are the aspirations and needs of small nations, but you've also got large nations who have the power," former Football Association chief executive Mark Palios told BBC Breakfast.

"It's not dissimilar to the attempts to form a European Super League. On one end you've got the people who create the cash, but on the other end you still need competition."

Rogers Byamukama of the Ugandan Football Federation argued that any avenue that could lead to more resources for nations like his should be explored.

"First and foremost, you need to understand that football is a very expensive venture, especially on the African continent where the resources are not easy to come by," he told Newsday on BBC World Service.

"For instance in Uganda, the number of infrastructure projects that have been funded by Fifa from the resources generated by Fifa, especially at the World Cup, both from ticket sales as well as sponsors.

"On top of that, there are many grassroot programmes that have been funded by Fifa, including schools for football.

"From my perspective, any avenue that brings in more resources is good because those resources would be distributed and given to federations, especially on the African continent and that would inspire growth."

Byamukama acknowledged Uefa's right to speak out, but suggested that its members are not reliant on Fifa funding like many associations in the rest of the world where Infantino remains popular.

In the first two cycles of the Fifa Forward development programme, through to 2022, $2.8bn (£2.08bn) was made available for investment across the 211 member associations.

Fifa Forward 3.0 - covering the years 2023 through to 2026 - has produced a 30% increase in funding.

Fifa has provided a further $5m (£3.7m) for every member association, with another $60m (£44.48m) paid to each confederation for their own projects.

After being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023, Infantino is expected to win another term in 2027.

fullText:
CHICAGO — Ten years ago Scott Harris was the 29-year-old director of baseball operations for the Chicago Cubs, doing whatever it took to win a championship.

That involved eating copious amounts of cake in the front-office suites at Wrigley Field, at the direction of his boss, then-Cubs President Theo Epstein.

As ESPN’s Wright Thompson wrote: “Their world up there has its own set of rules and superstitions, and central to the canon is this: If the team needs offense, Theo makes Scott Harris, the director of baseball operations, take out a loaf of plain bread and start eating. When Harris eats carbs, the Cubs score. One game, when the White Sox were no-hitting them, Theo got an entire chocolate cake from the passing dessert cart on the suite level. Harris ate more than half of it and the Cubs won.

“ ‘Harris,’ Theo says, taking a bag of bread and throwing it to Scott, knowing that the Cubs always need hot bats against the Cardinals. ‘Just start eating.' ”

Harris had his cake and ate it too.

He won a ring with the Cubs, became general manager of the San Francisco Giants and moved on to become president of the Detroit Tigers.

In that role, he might hold the keys to the Cubs’ chances of going back to the World Series for the first time since 2016. Harris happens to employ one of the two best pitchers on the planet in Tarik Skubal and reportedly is listening to offers leading into Monday’s MLB trade deadline.

One of the teams interested, according to a report by Patrick Mooney of The Athletic, is the Cubs, who are run by another former boss, Jed Hoyer, Epstein’s successor as president of baseball operations.

If you notice a twinkle in Hoyer’s eye Friday when the Cubs take on the New York Yankees at Wrigley Field, you can probably assume he has been Skubal diving all week, like several of his peers. He’s not dumb and knows there’s no cost in asking. He and Harris are old friends and compete annually for the Theo Cup, an imaginary trophy that theoretically goes to the winner of the Cubs-Tiger series.

But could the Cubs really put together a package that would satisfy Harris? History suggests they’ll shoot for the moon, settle for a middle-of-the-road starter and keep the prospects, explaining later that the price was too exorbitant.

Or maybe Harris simply could send Hoyer a non-negotiable list of players he demands, along with a chocolate cake and a post-it note saying, “Just start eating.” He’s in the driver’s seat and can just as easily send Skubal to the Milwaukee Brewers, the Cubs’ archrival, and team him up with Jacob Misiorowski for the best one-two punch in baseball.

The mere notion of the Cubs getting Skubal is seemingly fantasy-world stuff, based on Hoyer’s track record since taking the throne from Epstein in 2021. Truly elite starters are not usually on his radar. Jameson Taillon, Marcus Stroman and Shota Imanaga are the only starters he has given deals of three to four years, and Skubal’s agent is Scott Boras, so it’s certain he’ll go to free agency.

That makes Skubal a probable two-month rental for a slew of players. Harris will have several other bidders, including you know who — the team that prints money like the Cubs print Clark the Cub stickers.

ESPN’s Jeff Passan speculated the front-runner for Skubal is those same Los Angeles Dodgers — no surprise — since they have both the money and prospects and also would be willing to sign him to a long-term megadeal when the lockout ends.

To outbid their rivals, the Cubs likely would have to part with rehabbing starter Ben Brown and perhaps three top prospects, including No. 1 prospect Josiah Hartshorn. That’s not very appetizing, but neither was the price for Aroldis Chapman at the ’16 deadline, when Epstein swallowed hard and made the move,

Still, it’s not crazy to imagine Skubal pitching Tuesday night at Wrigley Field, when the Cubs play the Dodgers.

Which uniform he would be wearing is the real question.

Harris was not able to attend the recent reunion of the 2016 champions at Wrigley Field, but one of his top lieutenants was front and center. Newly hired Tigers special assistant Kyle Hendricks wasn’t sent on a reconnaissance mission by Harris, though he was on the stage when Chairman Tom Ricketts inaugurated the Champions Gate by noting “it has plenty of room for future champions.”

Tom, meet the Professor. He might be able to help you add another year to the gate.

Ricketts didn’t specifically mention this year’s team when addressing the empty space reserved for championships, but presumably he believes the future starts now.

The 2026 Cubs have weathered injuries, a 10-game losing streak and prolonged slumps by high-priced stars to put themselves in strong position for a wild-card spot at the very least. Pete Crow-Armstrong is having a special season, starters Matthew Boyd and Imanaga have been peaking of late and the defense remains the gold standard.

Adding Skubal to the mix would be the greatest needle drop of Hoyer’s career, bringing an instant jolt of energy to a fan base that has been waiting patiently for a team that can make a long October run.

Last year’s mini-run included five playoff home games during which Wrigley Field was turned up to 11. It was an instant flashback to how insane things were in 2015 and ‘16, when a city danced to the Cubs’ beat. “The Lovable Reunion” podcasts of Anthony Rizzo and David Ross are bittersweet reminders of how good Cubs fans had it and how badly it all ended when the stars were traded, nontendered, retired or fired.

After a 4-2, 10-inning win Thursday against the St. Louis Cardinals, the Cubs returned to start an important six-game homestand against the Yankees and Dodgers. It was already the most anticipated week of the year when the schedule was announced, and with Skubal’s name suddenly in the mix, the party-mode setting might never be turned off in Wrigleyville, barring some glitchy Wi-Fi.

Every season “is sacred,” Epstein said at the start of the original rebuild. Some are more sacred than others. So is this one of them?

If that’s the case, Cubs fans need to be loud and clear with their message to the decision-makers: How soon is now?

So go ahead, Jed. Eat that cake.

title: European football unites against FIFA proposal as UEFA approves boycott of all competitions
description: European football has approved a boycott of all FIFA competitions after UEFA's 55 member associations unanimously rejected Gianni Infantino's proposal to sell minority stakes linked to future FIFA World Cups to private investors. The decision was reached during an emergency meeting on Thursday and represents the strongest challenge yet to FIFA's plan to raise $20…
fullText:
UEFA's 55 member associations have agreed to boycott all FIFA competitions while Gianni Infantino's World Cup investment proposal remains active.

Concacaf has joined UEFA in rejecting the plan, creating significant opposition to FIFA's proposed $20 billion private equity deal.

The coordinated resistance places growing pressure on FIFA ahead of next year's presidential election.

European football has approved a boycott of all FIFA competitions after UEFA's 55 member associations unanimously rejected Gianni Infantino's proposal to sell minority stakes linked to future FIFA World Cups to private investors.

The decision was reached during an emergency meeting on Thursday and represents the strongest challenge yet to FIFA's plan to raise $20 billion through the sale of equity in FIFA Forward Enterprises, the organisation established to oversee the governing body's commercial and event operations.

UEFA confirmed that its member associations will not take part in FIFA competitions while the proposal remains active.

"UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions," the governing body said in a statement.

The move would prevent Europe's leading nations, including England, Germany, France and reigning world champions Spain, from competing in FIFA tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups, unless the proposal is withdrawn.

The opposition widened later on Thursday when Concacaf also voted to reject the proposal following a meeting of its 41 member associations.

Concacaf represents the United States, Canada and Mexico, the three host nations of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

The United States Soccer Federation publicly backed the confederation's position, stating that it "stands with Concacaf and its members."

Infantino announced the proposal earlier this week as part of plans to increase FIFA's commercial revenues through outside investment.

Under the proposal, investors would purchase minority, non-controlling interests in FIFA Forward Enterprises in return for involvement in future commercial and broadcasting revenues generated by FIFA competitions.

The investment group is backed by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared Kushner is the son-in-law of United States President Donald Trump.

FIFA projected that each of its 211 member associations could receive more than $80 million through 2037 if the proposal is approved.

Member associations had been given until Sept. 19 to support the proposal ahead of a planned vote.

UEFA's position followed a virtual meeting in which, according to sources, more than 50 national associations spoke against the proposal.

European football's governing body criticised both the substance of the plan and the process by which it had been introduced.

"Some things are simply too important to sell," UEFA said.

"The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."

UEFA also criticised FIFA for introducing the proposal without meaningful consultation.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football," the statement added.

Concacaf echoed many of those concerns following its own meeting.

The confederation said its members had raised concerns over the lack of due process, the shortened consultation period and the absence of approval through FIFA's established governance procedures.

Concacaf confirmed that its representatives on the FIFA Council would seek discussions with FIFA over alternative methods of increasing development funding while insisting that any future proposals must comply with FIFA's statutes.

Opposition also emerged in Asia.

Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa warned member associations that FIFA's approach risked damaging the structure of international football.

In a letter sent to AFC members, Sheikh Salman wrote that "FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football."

He added that such a proposal could not succeed without broad support from the continental confederations.

The growing resistance leaves Infantino facing the most significant political challenge of his presidency.

FIFA is scheduled to elect its next president in Rabat, Morocco, next March, with prospective candidates required to declare their intention to stand before the Nov. 18 deadline.

title: Vozinha's Colo Colo move delayed by 'personal matters': club
description: Vozinha, the goalkeeper who played a key role in Cape Verde's fairytale World Cup run, has delayed his arrival in Chile to sign for Colo Colo because of "personal matters," the club's sporting director said on Thursday.Colo Colo president Anibal Mosa had announced the signing of the 40-year-old keeper last Friday, later saying he would arrive in Chile on Thursday.
fullText:
Vozinha, the goalkeeper who played a key role in Cape Verde's fairytale World Cup run, has delayed his arrival in Chile to sign for Colo Colo because of "personal matters," the club's sporting director said on Thursday.

Colo Colo president Anibal Mosa had announced the signing of the 40-year-old keeper last Friday, later saying he would arrive in Chile on Thursday.

The delay fueled speculation in the local press, with some reporting that Vozinha was also in talks with Moroccan club RS Berkane.

"An additional period has been requested to resolve some personal matters ... and we’ll surely have news soon regarding his travel schedule," Jaime Pizarro, Colo Colo’s sporting director, told reporters.

Pizarro said immigration procedures were also a factor in the delay and that the club had accepted Vozinha's requests "to allow him to attend to his needs."

Vozinha starred at the World Cup with heroic displays in a 0-0 group-stage draw against eventual champions Spain and in a 3-2 extra-time loss to finalists Argentina in the knock-out rounds.

The keeper, whose full name is Josimar Jose Evora Dias, will move to Chile from Chaves of the Portuguese second division. Although he did not sign his first professional contract until he was 26, he has also played in Cyprus, Slovakia, Moldova and Angola.

His performance at the World Cup earned him worldwide fame, and his Instagram account jumped from 50,000 followers to more than 29 million.

title: PFL, Jake Paul’s MVP merge to form new global combat sports company
description: Professional Fighters League and Most Valuable Promotions have officially merged in a massive development in the world of combat sports.
fullText:
Professional Fighters League and Most Valuable Promotions have officially merged in a massive development in the world of combat sports.

 The new company will operate under the MVP banner, led by Co-Founders and Board Members Jake Paul and Nakisa Bidarian. Meanwhile, former PFL CEO John Martin will serve as CEO and Board Member of the new league. MVP’s boxing business and blockbuster live events will continue under Bidarian. Existing PFL shareholders 885 Capital and affiliated entities Knighthead Capital Management will be the founding investors of the new league, committing new capital.

 The new league vows to work under a “fighter-first” philosophy, seemingly challenging rival Ultimate Fighting Championship. While the UFC has been severely criticized over minimum profit share for athletes, the new combat sports league promises equitable compensation. The new league also plans to encourage athletes to build their brands inside and outside of competition, probably hinting at freedom to choose sponsors.

“We started MVP to disrupt a broken model,” Jake Paul, co-founder of Most Valuable Promotions, said in a press release. “We wanted to give fighters fair pay and a bigger, modernized stage to become global superstars. Joining forces with PFL accelerates that vision by a decade. We now have a scaled platform to give today's fans what they want: elite talent mixed with culture, lifestyle, and massive social velocity. MVP was always bigger than me and bigger than any one fighter. MVP is an inevitable movement that needs to happen for the athletes, and now we have all the resources we need to build something that changes this sport forever. I have more conviction in MVP than ever, driven by the proliferation of AI, which will only increase the value of real, live experiences and the sports properties that can bring fans closer to the athletes they love. I look forward to putting my entire promotional muscle into our new company, returning to the boxing ring and making my MVP MMA debut. To all current MVP and PFL fighters, things just got bigger. To fighters fighting in other organizations, we are open for business when you are contractually free. The time for change is now. Welcome to MVP.”

 The combined company also vows to display its capabilities by hosting five premium events across boxing and MMA in August. The brand will have 400 athletes combined under its roster and plans to invest aggressively in both sports.

 “Over the past seven years, PFL has built the world’s No. 2 global MMA company, assembling one of the sport’s most elite fighter rosters while creating a world-class global business with premier media distribution across 34 broadcast and streaming partners, reaching fans in more than 170 countries,” John Martin, chief executive officer of the new company said in a press release. “At the same time, MVP has redefined how combat sports connects with a new generation of fans, creating events that become cultural moments and proving that athletes, sports, entertainment and creators can all thrive together. This merger brings scale - in operations, in distribution and media rights, in sponsorship, in fighter development and in fan engagement. We're not just combining companies, we're bringing an entire combat sports community together and creating a more powerful platform to accelerate growth. One company, one global stage, millions of fans and we're only just getting started. I'm excited to work with Jake and Nakisa as we build the future of combat sports together, and I'm deeply grateful for the continued confidence and support of our lead investors, 885 Capital and Knighthead Capital Management.”

title: Canada celebrates new bridge to US while fighting Trump tariffs
description: Canadian officials are celebrating a new U.S.-Canada bridge over the Detroit River. The international span is expected to improve trade on both sides of the border and give travelers another route to both countries.
fullText:
Canada celebrated the completion of a new bridge to the U.S. over the Detroit River, a multibillion-dollar project that will serve as a critical path for trade, jobs and tourism between the countries. (AP video: Mike Householder)

The Gordie Howe International bridge connects Detroit and Windsor, Ontario is shown Friday, July 24, 2026, in Windsor. 

The Gordie Howe International bridge connecting Detroit and Windsor, Ontario is shown Friday, July 24, 2026, in Windsor. 

Gregor Robertson, Canadian Minister of Housing and Infrastructure gives thumbs up during a Canadian celebration for the Gordie Howe International bridge connecting Detroit and Windsor, Ontario Friday, July 24, 2026, in Windsor. 

A Canadian flag is displayed during a Canadian celebration marking the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which connects Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, on Friday, July 24, 2026, in Windsor, Ontario.. 

A truck is parked during a Canadian celebration marking the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which connects Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, on Friday, July 24, 2026, in Windsor, Ontario.

WINDSOR, Ontario (AP) — Canada on Friday celebrated the completion of a new bridge to the U.S. over the Detroit River, cutting a ceremonial ribbon on a multibillion-dollar, multiyear project that will serve as a critical path for trade, jobs and tourism between the countries.

As the six-lane Gordie Howe International Bridge dominated the skyline behind them, officials lined up in Windsor, Ontario, to hail what one described as “one of the most significant infrastructure achievements in Canada’s history.” The bridge opens to traffic on Monday.

“Some days are remembered because they mark the end of a journey. Others are remembered because they mark the beginning of something entirely new. Today is both,” said Chuck Andary, interim CEO of the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority, which will operate the bridge.

Missing from the event: U.S. and Michigan representatives. Canada scratched a joint gathering after President Donald Trump this week suddenly announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods entering the U.S. A soloist sang the national anthem, “O Canada,” but the U.S. anthem was not performed.

“Our relationship has been challenged over the last few years, and President Trump is threatening tariffs just this month. But team Canada has never been more united,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford told the crowd, which applauded at times during his defense of the country.

More than 70% of Canada’s exports go to the U.S., making America its largest trade partner, and Detroit is the No. 1 port for truck traffic on the U.S.-Canada border, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation.

The Howe bridge will instantly create competition. For nearly a century, the privately owned Ambassador Bridge has been the only route for large commercial trucks moving between the U.S. and Canada at Detroit. Businesses say the new span will be faster and less expensive.

The bridge is named for Howe, a Canadian icon — “Mr. Hockey” — who played on the other side of the Detroit River for the NHL’s Detroit Red Wings. He died in 2016. Ford and Mark Wiseman, the Canadian ambassador to the U.S., wore hockey sweaters with Howe’s No. 9.

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens repeatedly praised Howe and appeared to take a subtle dig at Trump. He said he recently texted Dr. Murray Howe to ask who might be his father’s target these days if he had to slam someone into the hockey boards.

“He’s a gentleman. He didn’t answer,” Dilkens said. “But I think we all know who that person might be if Gordie was going to check one person into the board.”

Surrounded by family, Murray Howe thanked residents of both countries and specifically named Canadian officials and the U.S. president. He recalled how his father grew up in Saskatchewan before moving to Ontario at age 16 for a tryout with the Red Wings.

“This bridge will serve as an unmistakable symbol of the priceless bond and true friendship between the people of Canada and the people of the United States,” Murray Howe said, expressing the same long-term view as other speakers.

Construction, which began in 2018, took years, partly because of a global slowdown caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Canada paid to build the bridge at an estimated cost of $6.4 billion. A recent agreement says Canada will share some toll revenue with the U.S. government for 15 years.

Trump praised his administration for that deal in a social media post while the Ontario event was in progress. “We changed the terms,” he said.

Michigan will also get a share, but not until Canada’s costs are recovered, likely decades from now.

The bridge is 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) long and rises 151 feet (46 meters) above the Detroit River at its highest point. Pedestrians and bicyclists carrying proper identification will be able to cross it for free in a few weeks.

title: State Department says it made ‘an unfortunate error’ when it mislabeled countries on map of Africa
description: The US State Department on Thursday said its use of a map that incorrectly labeled all the countries it identified on a map of Africa at an international conference this week was “an unfortunate error...
fullText:
The US State Department on Thursday said its use of a map that incorrectly labeled all the countries it identified on a map of Africa at an international conference this week was "an unfortunate error."

The map was shown during an event at the AIDS 2026 conference in Rio de Janeiro. It highlighted six countries on the continent: Nigeria, Mozambique, Uganda, Cote d'Ivoire, Malawi, and Cameroon. Not one of them was correctly identified by lines pointing from the names to the positions on the map. It showed coastal Nigeria as landlocked. Mozambique, which is in the southeast of the continent, was shown in the Horn of Africa. Cote d'Ivoire was shown on the wrong side of the continent.

A photo of the errant map was shared in a Substack post from AIDS expert Emily Bass. According to an analysis from Reuters, the map contained "an artificial intelligence watermark that ⁠signals it was made with OpenAI tools."

A State Department spokesperson said Thursday that "this was an unfortunate error caused by a team member who hastily altered the slide deck immediately before the presentation at the AIDS 2026 Conference."

"We take full responsibility for the confusion and misrepresentation it caused for attendees, including our African partners," the spokesperson said.

Since President Donald Trump took office again, the State Department has significantly cut its global health funding and underwent a restructuring which has seen a significant number of career experts lose their jobs.

Cameron Hudson, a former State Department and NSC official on Africa, said that the mistake is "a reflection of what happens when you fire ⅓ of the State Department, eliminate multiple layers of bureaucracy and have too junior staff performing work under-supervised."

"There isn't just a cost savings when eviscerating staff and expertise. There's a real cost in reputation and effectiveness," he posted on X. "I suspect many people don't actually care because they say it's Africa, but the same thing is happening with teams trying to negotiate nuclear deals with Iran. That should concern everyone."

title: Is Infantino finished? Could Uefa boycott World Cup? What happens now?
description: It's been a seismic 48 hours for football after Uefa threatened to boycott the World Cup and Concacaf rejected Gianni Infantino's funding plan - what happens now, and can Fifa's president survive?
fullText:
The bombshell statement landed at 16:00 BST on Thursday, 30 July.

In terms of impact, European football's governing body Uefa could not have gone any bigger.

"Uefa and its national associations will not participate in Fifa competitions," it said.

Eleven brutal words. The definitive reaction to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a 20% stake in a subsidiary company set up to run the world governing body's competitions, including the World Cup.

A company it is intended Fifa will run but that will be part-funded by private investors, including the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Joshua Kushner.

It feels as though no-one who matters knows how this situation is going to play out just yet.

"Not sure the detail was considered when deciding the overall policy," was the response from a senior European football source when asked what this decision means for the U20 Women's World Cup, starting on 5 September, being hosted by Poland and featuring plenty of European nations.

Uefa's boycott threat will be activated if Infantino's funding deal is accepted.

Given 19 September is the deadline for countries to accept Fifa's deal and bank $20m (£15m) on 1 January, in theory, countries could be pulling out of that tournament in the middle of the quarter-finals and before the semis.

After that, the next senior matches in a Fifa competition are the Women's World Cup play-offs in October, which feature England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland among others.

"Wales is involved in the play-offs for the Women's World Cup in the autumn, and it would be our first qualification for a World Cup," Uefa vice-president and ex-Wales international Laura McAllister told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Nobody can even countenance the thought of not being involved in those.

"But let's be clear here. This is not a problem of Uefa's making. It's a problem that Fifa have created. Nobody wants the players to suffer, and nobody wants nations to suffer when it comes to the most prestigious competitions.

"We've been pushed into this corner and that's Fifa's responsibility."

Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approved

Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?

Uefa threatens full Fifa boycott over World Cup sale plans

No-one can be certain what happens now. And no-one knows what the future for Infantino is.

Fifa is yet to respond to Uefa's statement, which was followed up by another from Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and hosted this year's World Cup, saying their 41 members rejected the proposals.

Yet, in a sense, it is not Fifa's argument.

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt is a Fifa vice-president. She spoke out against the plan at Uefa's emergency meeting on Thursday. The FA said it stands "shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues" on the matter.

Scottish FA president Mike Mulraney is also chair of Fifa's finance committee. The Scottish FA's statement said the organisation "agrees unequivocally" with Uefa's stance.

The repeated responses from those who have spoken out are of fury at the lack of proper consultation and lack of dialogue from Infantino, including with his Fifa colleagues, as much as with the proposals themselves.

"Anger," said one source, when asked for the prevailing mood at Uefa's emergency meeting.

Infantino became Fifa president in 2016 when he beat Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. The Swiss is due to stand for a fourth term in March.

Prior to this week, it had been anticipated he would be re-elected unopposed. FAs around the world, including some in Europe, have already confirmed their intention to support the 56-year-old.

But sources say in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.

Now there is talk of trying to find someone to stand against him.

The name of Nasser Al-Khelaifi has been mentioned. This is understandable. Qatari Al-Khelaifi is already one of the most powerful figures in football, not only through his status as president of back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain but his leadership of European clubs.

Previously known as the European Clubs' Association, Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.

Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to over 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.

In theory, he would be the best person to challenge Infantino. But he doesn't want to. "He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.

Historically, sitting Fifa presidents are not challenged in elections. The last president to lose an election was Englishman Sir Stanley Rous when he was beaten by Brazilian Joao Havelange in 1974.

"I don't know, in all honesty," said McAllister, when asked if Infantino will keep his job.

Former FA chairman David Bernstein was asked the same question by BBC Sport.

"In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door," Bernstein said.

"But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."

Former Uefa chief executive Lars-Christer Olsson told the BBC that Infantino has overplayed his hand and his position could be in trouble.

He suggested Fifa should instigate a reform where the presidency circulates around figures from different confederations "rather than giving people so much power" as it has done with Infantino and his predecessors, Switzerland's Sepp Blatter and Brazil's Havelange.

When asked if Infantino should be removed from his role, Olsson said: "I think that should be a new start for football."

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - Fifa's 'unlikely saviour'

Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan

While Uefa only covers 55 of Fifa's 211 national associations, in pure playing terms, it is the most powerful confederation by far.

In the last edition of the World Cup, the Women's World Cup and the Club World Cup - Fifa's flagship events - Uefa supplied three of the four semi-finalists.

If there was no European involvement in a Fifa competition, the commercial impact would be seismic and ensure there was virtually no chance of Infantino hitting the figures he has promised in a letter to the national associations, when he talked about a $40bn (£30bn) product.

David Bernstein feels a solution has to be found.

"I can't believe in the long term that there will be a schism because it would be a lose-lose for everybody," he said.

"Fifa can't afford not to have European nations play in their competitions and frankly Europe can't afford not to be part of it.

"On this occasion, Infantino's got to back down. This deal is not acceptable. It's a friends deal and it's not right. If they want to raise capital, there's other, better ways of doing it."

McAllister accuses Fifa of 'blackmail' over World Cup plan

title: Thitikul leads Open as Ryu and Kuwaki chase
description: World number two Jeeno Thitikul leads the first round of the AIG Women's Open by two shots after a spectacular seven-under 64 at Royal Lytham & St Anne's.
fullText:
-7 A Thitikul (Tha); -5 S Kuwaki (Jpn), H Ryu (Kor); -4 Y Noh (US), C Boutier (Fra); -3 C Iwai (Jpn), C Wannasaen (Tha); -2 P Martin (Esp), L Coughlin (US), C Hull (Eng), R Takeda (Jpn), M Saigo (Jpn), L Woad (Eng), S Tan (Sin).

Selected others: -1 A Hewson (Eng), E Rhodes (Eng), A Fuller (Eng), L Ko (NZ), +1 M Yamashita (Jpn), +2 N Korda.

World number two Jeeno Thitikul leads the first round of the AIG Women's Open by two shots after a spectacular seven-under 64 at Royal Lytham & St Anne's.

The 23-year-old has 11 top-10 finishes in majors but has never won one, and went bogey-free in a fine start to her latest attempt.

South Korea's Haeran Ryu, aiming to become only the fifth woman in history to claim three majors in a calendar year, is second alongside Japan's Shiho Kuwaki on five under.

England's Lottie Woad and Charley Hull are both on two under, while compatriot Alice Hewson led the tournament in the morning and finished one under.

"Winning one [major] doesn't mean I am going to have a really good, successful career," Thitikul said.

"Winning one doesn't mean much, I would rather be a consistent player, more than just winning one and then gone.

"Sometimes I had a hard time dealing with all the noise."

The world's best golfers performed well in the opening round, with world number one Nelly Korda one of the few stars to fall behind.

Korda remains off the pace after shooting a two-over-par 73 in a round that included four bogeys.

Hull responds to criticism of prank on caddie

Korda & Hull seek major glory - Women's Open tee times

Thailand's Thitikul, who was leapfrogged by Korda as world number one when she won the Chevron Championship in April, sunk seven birdies in a faultless round.

Her round included three straight birdies on the front nine and difficult par saves.

Earlier this month, Ryu, 25, claimed her second major in the space of two weeks at the Evian Championship.

That form continued as four birdies on the front nine quickly took her to the top of the leaderboard.

Despite a bogey on the 15th, Ryu finished with two birdies in the last three holes.

Last year's Open champion Miyu Yamashita shot one-over-par, while three-time major winner Lydia Ko is even par.

Royal Lytham & St Anne's has hosted the Women's Open twice and had British winners both times - Scotland's Catriona Matthew in 2009 and England's Georgia Hall in 2018 - and the class of 2026 are aiming to keep that run going.

Woad, 22, finished tied for seventh at this year's Chevron Championship, backing up top-10 finishes at last year's Open and Evian Championship.

Having coming in as one of the favourites, her bogey-free round of 69 leaves her well poised after day one.

"Good start. No bogeys, which is always a good round here. Hit a lot of fairways and a lot of greens. Didn't make too many putts," she said.

Hull, a five-time runner up in majors, had yet another near-miss in June's US Open and will be hoping to finally get over the line.

Four birdies on the front nine gave the 30-year-old an ideal start as she aims to go one better than her runner-up finishes in 2023 and 2025.

Despite sinking six birdies, four bogeys pegged back Hull, who showed great skill to save par from the bunker on the 18th.

"I was super nervous on the first tee. I was so nervous. It's even more nerve-wracking when you're having to hit an iron because you have to stripe an iron shot," Hull said.

"I missed quite a few putts today that I felt I should have holed, but I felt like I stayed in there pretty well considering how nervous I was, because I feel there was a lot of pressure on me out there."

Hall, the most recent British female player to win a major, is back playing after giving birth five months ago.

The 30-year-old endured a tough opening round to end the day five over.

Korda started the year with two major titles, and any talk of a career Grand Slam seemed ambitious, even by her own high standards.

However, as the LPGA recognises a player as having achieved the career Grand Slam by winning four of the five major titles, Korda's victory at the US Open in June has given her a chance to enter the history books.

The 28-year-old, playing alongside Ryu, got off to a slow start with bogeys on the second and third holes but recovered those shots to reach the back nine at even par.

From hoping for a career Grand Slam, Korda will now have to fight to make Friday's cut.

Four birdies on the front nine gave the 30-year-old an ideal start as she aims to go one better than her runner-up finishes in 2023 and 2025.

Despite sinking six birdies, four bogeys pegged back Hull, who showed great skill to save par from the bunker on the 18th.

"I was super nervous on the first tee. I was so nervous. It's even more nerve-wracking when you're having to hit an iron because you have to stripe an iron shot," Hull said.

"I missed quite a few putts today that I felt I should have holed, but I felt like I stayed in there pretty well considering how nervous I was, because I feel there was a lot of pressure on me out there."

Hall, the most recent British female player to win a major, is back playing after giving birth five months ago.

The 30-year-old endured a tough opening round to end the day five over.

Korda started the year with two major titles, and any talk of a career Grand Slam seemed ambitious, even by her own high standards.

However, as the LPGA recognises a player as having achieved the career Grand Slam by winning four of the five major titles, Korda's victory at the US Open in June has given her a chance to enter the history books.

The 28-year-old, playing alongside Ryu, got off to a slow start with bogeys on the second and third holes but recovered those shots to reach the back nine at even par.

From hoping for a career Grand Slam, Korda will now have to fight to make Friday's cut.

title: UEFA’s World Cup boycott explained – and what happens next?
description: Is this the end of the World Cup as we know it? fullText:
Is this the end of the World Cup as we know it?

On Thursday, European football’s governing body UEFA announced that its member nations are prepared to boycott future men’s and women’s World Cups.

The dramatic step was a response to plans set out by FIFA, the organisation which runs global football, to sell stakes in its tournaments to private investors. The dispute could have far-reaching consequences for players, fans and the powerbrokers involved.

Our writers explain what is going on and analyse what might happen next.

On Tuesday, it was revealed that FIFA wanted to set up a new private entity — called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) — to manage the commercial operations of its showpiece events, including the World Cup. As part of the plans, FIFA announced it was looking to sell a 21 per cent minority stake in FFE to outside investors. FIFA said the company was valued at $20billion (£14.8bn) by global bank JPMorgan Chase.

Thrive Capital, the company founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is expected to head up the proposed investor group.

To entice its 211 member associations, FIFA president Gianni Infantino said they would be in line to receive $40m in FIFA’s next four-year cycle if they backed his plans. He then gave them just 53 days to support the proposals — or miss out on the potential windfall.

For the plans to go through, however, FIFA needs a majority of its member associations and approval from the 37 members of the FIFA Council.

Coming just weeks after the conclusion of a World Cup dogged by controversy — including extortionate ticket prices, commercial breaks in each half dressed up as hydration breaks, President Trump intervening to overturn a red card for U.S. striker Folarin Balogun, and a surreal half-time show in the final — and following Infantino’s extraordinary Instagram meltdown, the proposals have only intensified criticism of FIFA and its boss.

As soon as the plans became public on Tuesday, UEFA issued a swift and scathing response, saying they “cross a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross”.

It went on to say how “the soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.”

UEFA and its 55 member associations later gathered for a virtual meeting on Thursday, with more than 40 associations speaking out against the proposals. They later put out an uncompromising new statement, saying no UEFA national teams would take part in any FIFA competition until the proposals were shelved.

“Some things are simply too important to sell,” it added. “The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

UEFA taking such a strong stance puts Infantino in a very sticky spot.

There was a call between the 41 Concacaf nations scheduled for today. In a previous statement, it said, “Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release. We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.”

The Asian confederation also said it was “disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it through the appropriate and established governance channels”.

Meanwhile the African confederation has called for its member associations to “examine” the proposals in full.

Those who spoke out in favour of FIFA’s plans included Czech FA president David Trunda — although he later performed a screeching U-turn — and Erick Thohir, the president of Indonesia’s football association, who also owns Oxford United in England’s League One, a club who have just been placed under a transfer embargo.

At the 1934 World Cup in Italy, defending champions Uruguay did not participate in protest at the low number of European teams who had travelled to the inaugural tournament they hosted four years earlier.

Uruguay again boycotted the 1938 World Cup, joining Argentina in protest after FIFA awarded the tournament to France rather than Argentina as hosts.

Meanwhile in 1966, no African nation took part in the World Cup hosted by England after they boycotted the qualifying competition in protest at FIFA allocating just one place between Africa, Asia and Oceania, compared to 10 for Europe.

Readers might think next summer seems far enough away that surely it cannot be impacted, but the European qualifying play-offs for the Women’s World Cup take place in October. If UEFA plans to boycott the World Cup, those matches surely cannot take place, as they would be attempting to qualify for a tournament in which they would not plan to compete.

Those play-offs include reigning European champions England and 2019 finalists the Netherlands, as well as Wales, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and Norway. Thirty-two teams in total would be impacted.

And if UEFA goes along with the boycott until next summer, it would mean reigning world champions Spain and reigning European champions England — both heavily fancied to lift the trophy next summer — would not be in attendance. In fact, six of the top 10 nations would not be in Brazil.

Women’s football will be the most impacted by UEFA’s boycott in the coming months. Four of the next five FIFA competitions are in the women’s game, the first arriving as soon as September with the Women’s Under-20s World Cup, hosted by UEFA member Poland between September 5 and  September 27.

The Women’s Under-17s World Cup, starting on October 17 and ending on November 8, is set to be held in Morocco while, on the men’s side, the Under-17s World Cup follows in November and will be hosted by Qatar.

The second iteration of the Women’s Champions Cup — a FIFA competition featuring the champion clubs from each of the six continental confederations, won by Arsenal in January — is due to take place in January 2027, with the first two matches to be played in the home stadium of a team involved in each match, and the final four games to be played in Miami, Florida.

And then it’s the big one: the Women’s World Cup in Brazil next summer.

But Poland hosting the first tournament to be impacted by the boycott is certainly gripping given they are members of UEFA and would require FIFA either to find a new host entirely or cancel the tournament, given the short notice involved.

No matter how you slice it, Europe has been the dominant force in men’s World Cup history.

European nations have won a record 13 of the 23 tournaments, including six of the past eight, and have provided most of the teams in the latter stages. This summer Argentina and Morocco were the only non-European quarter-finalists, in keeping with a historical pattern that has seen UEFA sides account for 69 per cent of teams at this stage and 71 per cent of semi-finalists.

While the United States have been the most successful side in the women’s tournament, winning four of its nine editions, Europe has rapidly caught up. Three UEFA sides have reached the past two finals, with Spain beating England to win the 2023 tournament.

On the men’s side, a World Cup shorn of Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal, Erling Haaland and Jude Bellingham would be a hollow shell of a tournament. Or, to put it in terms FIFA’s proposed investors might better understand, it would strip the competition of its most valuable assets.

German website Transfermarkt provides estimates of players’ values, and each of its 10 most valuable players hails from a European nation. Of the 104 players valued at €50million (£42.8m; $57.6m) or more, 77 play for UEFA sides. FIFA’s proposal aims to maximise the tournament’s commercial appeal, but without these star talents, the value of the enterprise would collapse.

Similarly, the women’s event would be lacking some truly stellar names. Aitana Bonmati, who has won the last three Ballons d’Or, would be absent, as would her Spain compatriot Alexia Putellas. England’s Leah Williamson, Lauren James and Alessia Russo, too.

In fact, the entire top 10 of last year’s Ballon d’Or Feminin (Bonmati, Mariona Caldentey, Russo, Putellas, Chloe Kelly, Patri Guijarro, Williamson, Ewa Pajor, Lucy Bronze and Hannah Hampton) would be unavailable for the tournament, not to mention exciting young talent in Norway’s Signe Gaupset or France’s Alice Sombath.

It would mean a World Cup without the world’s best, which is hardly what a World Cup should be.

Conor O’Neill and Megan Feringa

Damaging? This destroys it. There is no FIFA Forward Enterprise without European nations taking part in its competitions.

Critics of Infantino’s plan were heartened by the initial negative response it received from the confederations in Asia, Europe and North and Central America, but were worried that the tone of those responses was more “why is this the first we are hearing of this idea”, as opposed to “this is a dreadful idea, just stop”.

And those concerns about the strength of the opposition to Infantino grew when the likes of the English, French and German federations all put out statements that were more focused on the process than the principle.

They need not have worried, though. Because we now know that UEFA and its member associations were just taking a few moments to find their backbones and clear their throats.

This is another European Super League moment. European football has correctly realised that this idea cannot be allowed to gain momentum. If Infantino could have dragged this through to his September 19 deadline, it would have been too late to stop it. He would have had two thirds of the planet, at least, on board. So, Europe has gone nuclear. We will not come to play. And without us, what have you really got to sell?

If this outbreak of unity lasts the weekend, FFE is OFF.

A lot. FIFA is keen to talk up taking football to the world, and equally keen to keep expanding its showpiece, but it remains the case that European nations provide the bulk of the tournament’s quality and, thus, the World Cup’s appeal.

Six of this year’s eight quarter-finalists were UEFA nations, and since money is apparently the main thing football’s governing body pays attention to these days, a quick look at who took home the most in performance-based payments from the World Cup quite neatly highlights how crucial UEFA teams are to FIFA’s pièce de résistance.

After stripping out the $10million all 48 teams got for showing up this summer, and $2.5m in preparation fees, FIFA doled out $223m on a performance basis. UEFA’s 16 teams hoovered up $127m of that. Put another way: one-third of the teams took home nearly two-thirds of the performance-based payments.

A World Cup without those teams would be dramatically diminished.

It absolutely should, right? You cannot with one breath say you are not going to play in the next World Cup but then, in the next, say, “We would still like to host one, though”.

No, if this boycott is to mean anything, it has to be a total boycott. FIFA, its sponsors and broadcasters, and its potential investors, need to know that Europe is off the table if Infantino presses on with FFE.

The funny thing is, some in the game thought it was incredibly unhelpful to UEFA’s cause that the German FA gave an interview to, ahem, The Athletic about its wish to host the 2038 or 2042 men’s tournament the day before Infantino announced this plan.

But then, in the German FA’s defence, it clearly did not know what Infantino had been plotting. After all, its boss only sits on the FIFA Council and those guys are the last people Infantino speaks to about his plans.

Yeah, sure, but only if the rebel alliance starts to fracture.

Europe may only have 55 of the 211 votes at FIFA but it has a far, far bigger share of FIFA’s commercial value because its nations have been providing the lion’s share of the teams, players and winners of FIFA’s competitions forever. Only South America has come close to Europe’s outsized impact and influence.

If Europe stays united on this, Europe wins this row. If some of UEFA’s members start to think they might like $40million to pay off their debts, build their own St George’s Park or hire Pep Guardiola, then Infantino can turn this around.

But everything we are hearing suggests European football really means it. They don’t like the process or the principle. And that mirrors what most European football fans think, too.

Might this view upset those parts of the world that really liked this idea? Those parts of the world that look at the European game with envy and frustration? Those parts of the world that find Europeans a bit preachy and selfish?

Yes, yes and yes. But that does not mean Europe is wrong in this regard. Putting any philosophical objections to “selling the World Cup” to one side, this is not a very good deal for global football. If it wants to go down this road, it could do a lot better.

Some in Europe will also point out that the rest of global football will continue to think Europe needs taking down a peg or two regardless of whether this deal goes through or not, so Europe might as well take the brickbats and be right.

In almost any other business or walk of life, this would be a resignation matter. But Infantino deciding to fall on his sword would arguably be even more surprising than his attempt to sell a fifth of FIFA’s revenues to a group of investors led by Ivanka Trump’s brother-in-law.

Prior to this week’s Infantino brainwave, there seemed little to no chance that anyone would stand against him when the next election for a FIFA president takes place in Morocco in March.

That is not to say everyone loves him — they do not — but nobody believed anyone else would stand a chance in that election, so what was the point?

Is that still the case now? Let us see how he responds to UEFA’s surprisingly strident rejection of this idea.

If he shrugs and says, “OK, I’ve heard you, we won’t do it — it was just a consultation exercise, anyway”, he very probably survives. He has done this type of thing a few times before and bounced back every time, usually with a new idea.

It is entirely possible, for example, that he quickly admits defeat on this one but then quickly comes back and says, “Right, Europe, you didn’t like that idea but FIFA has got to even the playing-field somehow, so let’s have 64-team World Cups with more money and slots for Africa and Asia”. That would be very on brand.

But if he ploughs on with FFE, hoping that UEFA starts to crumble… well, it becomes a case of last-man standing: him or Aleksander Ceferin, and Ceferin has the better weapons at the moment.

That does not mean that Ceferin would be the most likely successor to Infantino, though. For the reasons outlined above, he is not that popular outside Europe and he has not hidden his disdain for FIFA politics very well.

This is why seasoned FIFA watchers believe Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Qatari boss of beIN Media and the president of European Football Clubs, is a far better shout as he spans Asia and Europe, as well as big clubs and media partners.

title: ‘Football is not for sale’: Uefa confirms boycott of World Cup and Fifa competitions
description: ‘No Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition’ while Gianni Infantino’s plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup remain alive, says the organisation
fullText:
Football’s European governing body has announced a full boycott of Fifa competitions, including the World Cup, if Gianni Infantino’s controversial plans to sell off stakes in its tournaments to private investors are voted through.

The drastic action, which follows an emergency meeting on Thursday, was “unanimously” agreed among all 55 of Uefa’s member associations. A statement confirmed that “no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive”.

World Cup boycott latest: Uefa agree emergency action after Infantino sell-off plan

Uefa carries significant leverage as a World Cup without major nations such as champions Spain, France, England and Germany would compromise Infantino’s designs on extracting as much revenue from the global showpiece as possible. Six of the eight quarter-finalists from this summer’s World Cup were European.

It would also harm next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil, with Spain the reigning winners and European champions England also bringing considerable commercial interest in the tournament. England, runners-up at the 2023 World Cup, face two-legged qualification play-offs in October, as do Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

A spokeswoman for the English FA echoed the Uefa sentiment, saying: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose Fifa’s plans – the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will.”

Meanwhile, the majority of the 2030 World Cup will be staged in Europe, with Spain and Portugal sharing hosting rights along with Morocco, following games in South America hosted by Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay to commemorate the tournament’s centenary year.

On Tuesday, Fifa revealed plans to create a new $20bn subsidiary, 20 per cent owned by private investors, to manage the commercial rights and delivery of the World Cup and other major tournaments. Thrive Eternal, led by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is set to lead the new investment.

“This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa’s duty as the custodian of world football,” Uefa said. “The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in Fifa competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure.”

In a letter to the member associations, Infantino promised that national federations would benefit from an increase of its “Fifa Forward” funding from around $8m to $20m for the upcoming four-year cycle between 2027 and 2031 if the new FFE subsidiary is created.

Additionally, the letter states that a “one-off” payment of another $20m would be made available for member associations who vote for Infantino’s proposals on 19 September. Member associations are then warned that their funding for the 2027-2031 cycle would only stand at $10m if the vote does not pass, meaning they would miss out on $30m.

Uefa’s statement added: “National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.”

Many of the world’s smaller countries, especially those outside of Europe, are more dependent on funding from Fifa to run their national teams, develop long-term grassroots projects and invest in infrastructure, like pitches, academies and stadiums. Before this year’s World Cup, Infantino claimed that “without Fifa, there would be no football in 150 countries in the world”.

Uefa’s confirmation that it would stage a boycott comes ahead of a vote between Fifa’s 211 member associations on 19 September. Infantino’s proposals only require a majority vote of above 50 per cent, as well as backing from the Fifa Council, which means Uefa still requires more support from another federation, such as North America or Asia, to have a chance at winning the vote and avoiding a boycott.

“Uefa and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

“It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game. This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa’s duty as the custodian of world football.

“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.

“But our opposition goes far beyond process.

“The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in Fifa competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure. From that moment onwards, every decision on the international calendar, every decision on competition formats and every decision shaping the future of football is no longer driven by what best serves the game, but by what best serves shareholders.

“This model has no place in world football. Football’s future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return. Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain.

“Europe’s position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.

“Nobody should be in any doubt: Uefa and its national associations will oppose these plans with absolute determination.

“There are moments when institutions are judged not by what they are prepared to accept, but by what they refuse to compromise. This is one of those moments.

“Some things are simply too important to sell. The Fifa World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

title: McAllister accuses FIFA of 'blackmail' over World Cup plan
description: Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister has accused Fifa of trying to blackmail member associations into trying to accept its controversial private equity plan.
fullText:
Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister has accused Fifa of trying to blackmail member associations into trying to accept its controversial private equity plan.

European football's governing body has made a definitive stance against the Fifa proposals to sell stakes in major competitions.

The position was backed up when Uefa's 55 member associations voted to boycott the World Cup in response.

That was despite Fifa president Gianni Infantino writing to all national associations offer £15m to accept the offer by 19 September, with the promise of a further £15m to follow.

But, following Thursday's vote, former Wales international McAllister said there was unity and a strong sense of feeling between all Uefa nations about what she called a "genuine existential threat to the game" and "a ridiculous proposal".

"Effectively it's a form of blackmail financially to present the national associations with such a tight time period to consider such a significant seismic proposal," said McAllister, who sits on Uefa's executive committee.

"I think that's part of the problem, but not the root of the problem. The root of the problem is trying to sell off parts of football to a private equity environment.

"This poses a genuine existential threat to the game because the minute you sell off part of the crown jewels of football, clearly private equity has very different objectives and motivations to those of us who are custodians of the game."

Uefa to boycott World Cups if Fifa plans approved

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Uefa's boycott would cover all Fifa competitions - including the men's and women's World Cups and Club World Cup - and be triggered if Fifa president Gianni Infantino's proposals are voted through by member associations across the globe.

It would see a quarter of Fifa's members refusing to feature, including some of the world's biggest and most successful nations.

McAllister, who was elected to the position in 2023, admitted she hoped the boycotts do not come to pass – but warned it was not an empty threat.

"I feel optimistic they won't, because the reality is the powerhouse of world football is Europe," she told BBC Radio Wales Drive.

"So by taking the very powerful clear and categorical stance we've taken, hopefully we've given some confidence to the other confederations that they can follow suit, and that together we can defeat the proposal.

"This is not an empty threat because we have to be prepared to follow through on it, but I find it incredible that FIFA would consider pushing on with World Cups without European nations there."

McAllister also urged urged other governing bodies to push back on the controversial plans.

"I very much hope it will not come to a boycott and I find it hard to imagine that FIFA will want to push us into that situation and there's a number of reasons for that - one being the status of European nations in world football," McAllister told BBC Radio 4's PM show.

"A World Cup without Europe isn't a World Cup at all.

"There is now a timescale involved which can be rescinded. There are other confederations such as the Asian and Central and North American confederations who have already made their concerns known.

If the situation continues, I think the stance we've taken today will give some incentive to the rest of the world of football to stand up to this awful proposal."

She also accused FIFA, and Infantino, of being primarily motivated by money, and cited other examples of questionable interventions that has prompted scepticism within UEFA.

"I can only speak from a UEFA standpoint, but this isn't the only one that has caused us a problem.

"The overturning of the red card, the so-called FIFA peace prize, all of that has caused us quite some concern from a European standpoint."

Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?

Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan

Football Association of Wales chief executive Noel Mooney was among those to voice their concerns at the emergency meeting held virtually on Thursday.

There are now questions over the UK bid for the Women's World Cup in 2035. The joint bid by England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales was the only valid submission for the 48-team tournament, with confirmation of host status set to be delivered in November.

Prior to that, all four nations will be involved in play-offs for the 2027 World Cup.

McAllister, a former Wales captain, added: "We've got a lot of stages before that; you don't need to tell me how significant that is for Rhian Wilkinson and the girls.

"It's something that I've worked towards for all of my career in sports administration and as a player, but I don't think it will come to that because Europe really holds most of the cards in terms of how the World Cup can operate and its financial viability.

"Imagine a Women's World Cup without Spain, without England, without France, without Germany and the same would apply to the men."

title: Wu edges past Murphy into Shanghai semi-finals
description: World champion Wu Yize overcomes "a lot of mistakes" to edge past Shaun Murphy 6-5 and reach the Shanghai Masters semi-finals.
fullText:
World champion Wu Yize overcame "a lot of mistakes" to edge past Shaun Murphy 6-5 and reach the Shanghai Masters semi-finals.

Meeting for the first time since Wu won the dramatic World Championship final in May, the 22-year-old trailed by five frames to four in the third round, having led 3-1, before building his fifth 50-plus break of the match to force a decider.

After England's Murphy unexpectedly missed a red when leading 62-29 in the final frame, the Chinese held his nerve to clear the black and complete another nail-biting win.

Wu will face England's Judd Trump in the last four after he brushed aside Scotland's John Higgins 6-0, including three consecutive century breaks in the final three frames.

"Although the result was good and I managed to win the match, I never really took control of it. Hopefully I can find my rhythm and get back to my best in the next match as I prepare for the semi-finals," said Wu.

"I definitely made a lot of mistakes that I shouldn't have made. To be honest, I didn't expect to get another chance in the deciding frame, and I was quite surprised when Shaun missed and let me in.

"I don't think either of us played particularly well today. It wasn't as high a standard as the match we produced in the World Championship final."

Defending champion Kyren Wilson recovered from 5-3 down to beat three-time world champion Mark Williams in a deciding frame, reeling off breaks of 61, 54 and 113 to complete his comeback.

He will face 2025 world champion Zhao Xintong in a repeat of last year's semi-final, which Wilson won 10-5.

Zhao crushed Australia's Neil Robertson 6-0, with a highest break of 117 in the third frame.

title: Littler's nan shocked by seeing mural from bus
description: A mural in Warrington honouring two-time world darts champion Luke Littler surprises his grandmother after she spots it while on a local bus.
fullText:
A mural in Warrington honouring two-time world darts champion Luke Littler left his grandmother shocked after she spotted it while on a local bus.

Littler, 19, watched on Thursday as the mural, placed on the side of Golden Square Shopping Centre, was unveiled.

But on Wednesday, Littler's grandmother was on a bus that passed the mural as it was being prepared for the ceremony. She got off to look at it before contacting other members of the family.

"I think my nan was on the bus yesterday," said Littler, speaking to BBC Sport's Nesta McGregor. "She actually came down here, she got off the bus and spoke to the guys that were doing it. Then, she phoned my dad and that's how I found out.

"She was here before us. Unbelievable. I think that was always going to happen really.

"Very happy, family's happy, we're happy. I was just never going to turn it down really.

"It's a great honour. It's good to see so many people here as well. I was expecting a fair few people, but it's a 'pinch me' moment. I can't believe his happened."

The mural unveiling happened days after Littler won the 2026 World Matchplay - his 11th PDC major title. Only Phil Taylor and Michael van Gerwen have more.

While Littler could yet end 2026 by winning every major title in a calendar year, Van Gerwen has dropped from fourth to seventh in the PDC's Order of Merit in recent days.

It is the first time he has been outside the world's top four since 2013 - but Littler hopes the Dutchman can rediscover his form to compete with him, as well as Luke Humphries and Gian van Veen, the only three players in the world to have earned more than £1m in prize money in the past two years.

"We're seeing Van Gerwen at the minute who is not playing at his best game - he's down to seventh in the world now is Michael," Littler added.

"Personally, I want Michael to get back to his best. He needs to get back to his best to compete with us."
